definitions.definitionEn: Strictly thermodynamic entropy. A measure of the amount of energy in a physical system that cannot be used to do work.

example.en: Ludwig Boltzmann defined entropy as being directly proportional to the natural logarithm of the number of microstates yielding an equivalent thermodynamic macrostate (with the eponymous constant of proportionality). Assuming (by the fundamental postulate of statistical mechanics), that all microstates are equally probable, this means, on the one hand, that macrostates with higher entropy are more probable, and on the other hand, that for such macrostates, the quantity of information required to describe a particular one of its microstates will be higher. That is, the Shannon entropy of a macrostate would be directly proportional to the logarithm of the number of equivalent microstates (making it up). In other words, thermodynamic and informational entropies are rather compatible, which shouldn't be surprising since Claude Shannon derived the notation 'H' for information entropy from Boltzmann's H-theorem.
example.ja: ルートヴィヒ・ボルトマンはエントロピーを、同程度の熱力学的マクロの状態を生じるマイクロソフトの自然対数に直接比例するものと定義した. (基本的には統計的力学の定理による) 全てのマイクロ状態が同等の可能性を持ち、一方では高密度のマクロの状態にあるマクロの状態はより高い確率を持ち、一方で、そのようなマクロの状態の指定に必要な量は、ある特定のマクロの状態に比例する。また、あるマクロの状態がより高い状態を記述するために必要な情報の量とみなす。
